declared.title: Does Valuing Happiness Lead to Well-Being?

population: Dutch adults of a population panel (LISS), five yearly waves, 2019 to 2023

findings.text: Adults who valued happiness more were on average more satisfied with life, with more positive and less negative feelings

support.sentence: Random-intercept cross-lagged panel models indicated that those who valued happiness generally exhibited higher well-being as manifested by life satisfaction, more positive affect, and less negative affect.

findings.text: When a person came to value happiness more, their life satisfaction a year later did not change, and they felt both more positive and more negative feelings

support.sentence: However, increases in valuing happiness did not result in changes in life satisfaction 1 year later and had mixed emotional consequences (i.e., increasing both positive and negative affect).

limits: valuing happiness is one item (happiness as a guiding value, 1 to 7), near its ceiling: mean 6.1, SD 1.0 in 2019 (preprint, Table 1)
the emotional cost: valuing it more is followed by a little more negative affect too (published abstract); affect models exploratory (preprint)
observational: changes within a person, never a manipulation; small effects
the Netherlands only; 8,331 people over five waves, about 5,000 to 5,900 answers a year
